source.title: Cross-seed explainability using Procrustes-conditioned Joint End-to-end Top-K Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: None; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-seed similarity of SAE features in BERT using a different method from toy-model superposition experiments. This bears on indirect evidence for recoverable, repeatable features, but it does not test the original toy-network geometry directly.
record.gate_note: The results test whether SAE feature activations align across independently seeded BERT models, and how the alignment/training condition affects that. The paper reports a separate five-seed-pair aggregate for each Table 1 dataset and condition. The appendix also reports per-pair universal-feature counts for rotation controls. Its 500-datapoint alignment sample size and alignment diagnostics are not outcomes about the claim. The qualitative ablation of one feature concerns feature interpretation, not cross-seed stability or canonicality.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It uses SAEs as a tool to propose a Procrustes-conditioned joint Top-K SAE and reports how its pipeline compares with SAE baselines. Its measure is how well SAE features correlate across independently fine-tuned BERT models (seeds 42/137, 99/7 and so on), which is cross-model feature universality. It does not measure SAE stability or completeness on one model (V5), sparse feature recovery versus a non-SAE reference (V4), or any toy-model, capacity or dimensionality question (V1–V3, V6). The joint-SAE conditions also train toward shared features by design: one shared encoder, plus a cross-loss that directly penalises differences between the two seeds' sparse codes. Their high correlations are therefore partly built in rather than observed.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim Procrustes-conditioned joint Top-K SAEs yield highly correlated 'universal' features across BERT seeds. Post-hoc rotation of independent SAEs gives no consistent benefit, and rotation helps only when it conditions joint training. The full pipeline gives the most universal features on two of three datasets (on TweetEval rotation-only has 405 versus 398). They acknowledge a single model family and only anecdotal feature interpretation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Procrustes alignment followed by joint Top-K end-to-end SAE training on BERT activations; it is not a reproduction of toy-model superposition experiments. The described approach combines alignment, joint training, and cross-seed SAE losses.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by dataset and SAE condition. Joint training with Procrustes outperforms joint training without rotation; post-hoc rotation does not reliably help. The full cross-loss condition changes the results only slightly relative to rotation-only and does not increase every universal-feature count. The paper also states that SAE results can vary by layer and discusses using layer 10 of 12.

fits_no_version.finding: Independently trained SAEs on differently seeded fine-tuned BERT models share only part of their features after Hungarian matching. Top-100 r is 0.482 (Politeness), 0.363 (SST-2) and 0.511 (TweetEval). Universal features (r≥0.70) are 16.1%, 5.0% and 9.8% of features active in both models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features are largely universal across independently trained models of the same architecture.

record.problems: Only one BERT model family is tested. The principal Table 1 results aggregate five seed pairs; the appendix rotation-control table reports only two seed pairs per dataset. Feature interpretation is described as minimal and anecdotal, and the authors say broader model-family tests and rigorous interpretability evaluation are needed. The reported results concern activation correlations and universal-feature counts, not feature completeness or canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted Table 1 Top-10 correlations, universal-feature percentages, dead-feature fractions, and accuracy changes; omitted Appendix C3 mean-pooled SAE results; omitted Table D4 other than its per-pair universal counts for identity, true, mismatched, and maximum-random rotations. The retained Table 1 results include Top-100 correlations and universal-feature counts for all datasets and conditions.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, phase transition or superposition geometry.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions for important features.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
SAEs are used as a tool. There is no test of whether features are spread across neurons or of sparse-feature recoverability against a reference.
No SAE-seed stability on a fixed model, no completeness test, no canonicality test. The cross-seed comparison is across different BERT models.
No test of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: I override the reader's 'tests'/T2 labels: this is a methods paper (T4). Its joint conditions build in cross-seed agreement through a shared encoder and the cross-loss, so their results show method performance rather than evidence about any version. The independent-matched baseline is the only genuine measurement, and it concerns cross-model universality, not a listed version. Fig. 3's mean absolute cosine of 0.04 describes SAE decoder directions, not the model's feature geometry.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparse-feature overload sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular superposition geometry is tested.
The study does not test polysemanticity as competition for capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The study evaluates SAE feature correlations across BERT seeds, not feature spreading across neurons in LLMs generally, and does not establish how complete the recovered features are.
It tests cross-seed similarity under selected training and alignment methods, not whether SAE features are complete, canonical, or stable across other models, layers, or methods.
It does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional structures.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Joint SAE conditions, especially Procrustes rotation, across Politeness, SST-2, and TweetEval
reader_labels.reason: The study finds positive cross-seed feature correlations and universal features in joint SAE results; rotation-only and full conditions outperform no-rotation joint training on the reported Table 1 measures (r07–r12, r19–r24, r31–r36).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Independent SAEs and post-hoc rotation, across all three datasets
reader_labels.reason: Raw index matching gives near-zero correlations; matching yields some shared features, while post-hoc rotation gives inconsistent or lower results than matched SAEs (r01–r06, r13–r18, r25–r30).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: True Procrustes rotation with joint training, in the tested BERT seed pairs
reader_labels.reason: Cross-seed feature correlations and universal-feature counts are substantial in joint rotation conditions; the appendix reports true rotation exceeds identity, shuffled-correspondence, and random-rotation controls (r09–r12, r21–r24, r33–r36, r37–r60).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across datasets and SAE alignment/training choices
reader_labels.reason: Cross-seed similarity depends on matching, joint training, and rotation; post-hoc rotation does not reliably improve results, and full training does not increase every reported count over rotation-only (r03–r06, r15–r18, r27–r30, r35–r36). The study does not establish completeness or canonicality.
